title: The Person Who Weaponized Religion
paragraphs:
The Person Who Weaponized Religion
He knew every rule, defended every tradition, and believed he was serving God... until he discovered he was fighting against the very Messiah he claimed to honor.
There is something terrifying about being sincerely wrong.
Not because you intended evil.
Not because you hated God.
But because you loved your version of God so much that you stopped recognizing Him when He stood directly in front of you.
That was the scandal of Saul of Tarsus.

Long before he became the Apostle Paul, before churches were planted, before letters were written, before miracles were performed, Saul was a religious celebrity in the making. He was educated, respected, disciplined, zealous, and completely convinced he was on God's side.
If Saul lived today, many believers would probably admire him.
He knew Scripture.
He defended truth.
He opposed what he believed was heresy.
He was passionate.
Committed.
Fearless.
And completely blind.
That is what makes his story so frighteningly relatable.
Because the greatest danger to the soul is not always rebellion.
Sometimes it is religion without Christ.
Sometimes it is truth without love.
Sometimes it is defending God while resisting the work of God.
Saul first appears in Scripture during the murder of Stephen.
Acts 8:1 records:
"And Saul approved of his execution."
The Greek text says:
"Σαῦλος δὲ ἦν συνευδοκῶν τῇ ἀναιρέσει αὐτοῦ"
(Saulos de ēn syneudokōn tē anairesei autou)
Literally:
"Saul was giving approval to his destruction."
He was not merely present.
He was pleased.
He believed righteousness was being defended.
He believed he was protecting God's honor.
He believed violence was justified if it preserved religious purity.
History has seen this tragedy repeated countless times.
People have burned others in the name of God.
Condemned others in the name of God.
Excluded others in the name of God.
Destroyed others in the name of God.
All while believing they were serving God.
Jesus warned this would happen.
In John 16:2, He said:
"They will put you out of the synagogues. Indeed, the hour is coming when whoever kills you will think he is offering service to God."
The Greek phrase is:
"λατρείαν προσφέρειν τῷ Θεῷ"
(latreian prospherein tō Theō)
Meaning:
"to present worship or sacred service to God."
Imagine that.
Thinking you are worshiping God while opposing what God is doing.
That was Saul.
Religion had become a weapon.
Scripture had become ammunition.
Conviction had become cruelty.
The law had become a shield protecting his pride.
Yet beneath all his certainty was a desperate problem.
He knew about God.
But he did not know Christ.
And without Christ, even religion can become dangerous.
Then came the road to Damascus.
One moment Saul was hunting Christians.
The next moment heaven interrupted him.
Acts 9:3-4 says:
"Suddenly a light from heaven shone around him. And falling to the ground he heard a voice saying to him, 'Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting Me?'"
Notice what Jesus did not ask.
He did not say:
"Why are you persecuting My followers?"
He said:
"Why are you persecuting Me?"
Because Christ is so united with His people that what is done to them is done to Him.
Saul thought he was attacking Christians.
Jesus revealed he was attacking Christ Himself.
Everything changed with one question.
A question powerful enough to shatter decades of religious certainty.
A question many of us still need to hear.
Could it be possible that some of the things we defend most passionately are actually keeping us from seeing Jesus clearly?
Could it be possible that our traditions, preferences, pride, political loyalties, denominational identities, or religious habits sometimes become more important than Christ Himself?
Saul discovered that being convinced is not the same as being correct.
The Hebrew Scriptures had always pointed to Jesus.
Isaiah pointed to Him.
The Psalms pointed to Him.
The sacrifices pointed to Him.
The prophets pointed to Him.
Everything pointed to Him.
Yet Saul missed Him.
How?
Because knowledge without surrender produces blindness.
The Hebrew word often translated "know" is יָדַע (yada).
It means far more than intellectual awareness.
It means intimate relationship.
Experiential knowledge.
Personal encounter.
Saul had information.
What he lacked was transformation.
Many people today are exactly where Saul once stood.
They know verses.
They know sermons.
They know theology.
But they do not truly know Jesus.
And the distance between knowing about Christ and knowing Christ is the distance between death and life.
Then comes one of the most beautiful moments in all of Scripture.
Jesus could have destroyed Saul.
He could have judged him instantly.
He could have condemned him for every Christian imprisoned, beaten, or killed.
Instead, Jesus pursued him.
Grace found the man who least deserved it.
That is the Gospel.
Not that good people find God.
But that God finds sinners.
Paul would later write:
(1 Timothy 1:15)
Notice he did not say he was formerly the foremost.
Even years later, Paul never forgot the scandal of his past.
He never stopped marveling at grace.
Because those who understand how much they have been forgiven rarely become proud.
They become grateful.
The story of Saul becoming Paul is not merely a conversion story.
It is a resurrection story.
A story proving nobody is beyond redemption.
Not the addict.
Not the adulterer.
Not the skeptic.
Not the hypocrite.
Not the religious legalist.
Not the church critic.
Not the person carrying decades of shame.
Not even the person who once fought against Jesus.
Because the Gospel specializes in impossible transformations.
That is why our ministry exists.
Because we believe there are countless modern-day Sauls scrolling right now.
People exhausted from pretending.
People hiding behind religion.
People carrying guilt.
People who think their failures have permanently defined them.
People who believe their story is over.
But Jesus still rewrites stories.
That is what He does.
From blindness to sight.
From condemnation to forgiveness.
From death to life.
Maybe that is why this article found you today.
Not by accident.
Not by coincidence.
But because God is still asking the same question He asked Saul.
Are you willing to surrender everything you think you know and truly follow Jesus?
You may need it again during a season when pride tries to disguise itself as righteousness.

Someone in your family, a friend, a struggling believer, a prodigal son or daughter, or even someone who has been wounded by religion may desperately need this reminder that Jesus still transforms lives.
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else needs today.

More importantly, your support helps place Gospel-centered content in front of people who may never walk into a church but may encounter Jesus through a shared post, an article, a testimony, or a message of hope.

If God has used this ministry to bless you, supporting and sharing its work is one meaningful way to help spread the Gospel and steward the resources He has entrusted to us. Not because salvation can be purchased, earned, or supported financially—it cannot. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone (Ephesians 2:8-9). Rather, supporting Gospel ministry is one way believers participate in advancing the message of Christ to others.
Because one shared article can reach a wandering soul.
One testimony can break someone's silence.
One act of obedience can become part of another person's rescue story.
And one encounter with Jesus can rewrite everything.
The same Savior who stopped Saul on a dusty road is still stopping people in the middle of their rebellion, pride, confusion, religion, shame, and brokenness today.
The greatest miracle was never that Saul became Paul.
The greatest miracle was that Jesus loved Saul before Saul ever loved Jesus.
And He still does the same for us.
The grace you have been running from may be the very thing running after you.
